---
title: "Topic Modeling Slave Narratives"
subtitle: "A classroom-friendly guide to BERTopic, local models, topic labels, and interpretation"
---

The North American Slave Narratives collection, hosted by Documenting the American South at the University of North Carolina, preserves over 290 first-person accounts of enslaved life in the United States. Topic modeling gives us a way to search for recurring themes across the collection without reading every document from start to finish — and then to ask whether those themes shift across the decades in which the narratives were published.

This lesson introduces that workflow using a 10% sample of the collection. It is designed for students who may have little or no coding experience.

Use the pages below to learn the main ideas, run the workflow, download the result tables, and interpret the visualizations.

## Featured Visualization

This chart shows the largest topics across publication decades. The dates are publication dates, not necessarily the dates when narrated events happened.

```{=html}
<iframe class="viz-frame" title="Topic shares by publication decade" src="outputs/bertopic_sample_nomic_sensitive_lemmatized/metadata_visualizations/topic_prevalence_grouped_bars.html" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

In this sample, the 1830s are strongly shaped by abolitionist testimony, especially physical punishment and treatment by slaveholders. The 1900s and 1910s include more topics connected to Booker T. Washington, Tuskegee, education, churches, and public life.

## Result Tables

The result tables are CSV files. CSV means comma-separated values, a common spreadsheet format that can be opened in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers, or a text editor.

- `topic_review_table.csv`: best starting point for reviewing topic labels, top words, years, and contributing documents.
- `topic_labels_llm.csv`: topic labels and top words.
- `topic_assignments.csv`: which chunk was assigned to which topic.
- `sample_documents.csv`: which 29 documents were used in the 10% sample.
